docs.title: Quá trình làm
docs.text:
ấn tượng đầu tiên về web là nó là 1 web upload file.

-> tra gg upload file vulnerability: cơ bản là upload 1 file executable và trick server execute nó.

ở đây t sẽ đẩy 1 file .php (lý do nhìn ở các route, rất nhiều file .php -> server đang chạy = ngôn ngữ php, đẩy file .php lên có khả năng chạy được)

tuy nhiên thử đẩy .php file thì bị lỗi 'file type not allowed'. khá rõ ràng họ có cơ chế block

-> thử fuzzing = ffuf + list file extension AI. tuy nhiên là cái rabbit hole vì không thu lại được gì (không đẩy lên được, có đẩy lên được thì cũng chỉ toàn file có đuôi mà apache không tự động execute được)

đổi hướng: chuyển qua fuzzing routes. vẫn như cũ, ffuf + list AI gen

trong lúc chờ đợi thì mình đi mò tay xem nó có những có gì trước (dưới là note lúc đang làm bài):

/index.php; 
/uploads; 
/upload.php("file type not allowed", appear when attempts to upload .php or .PHP or anything like that); 
/exists.php?file=abc(response back with a simple json file {"file":"abc","exists":false}); 
/download.php?id=a1fe58ea (happens whenever i tried to click download); 
/uploads/new.txt (when i clicked download a uploaded file, seems to be called when /download.php?id=0d626dfe happens); 
/delete.php (POST request to this to delete a uploaded file, the body of the request is id=0d626dfe the id of the file); 
/rename.php (the body is id=a1fe58ea&to=no.py, interesting thing is on the index.php it doesnt change the name, but download the file and the name is changed)
i found some of the routes are 403. one of them is /uploads

sau đó so khớp với kết quả fuzzing thấy khớp.

và có lẽ là intentional, tác giả để folder .git đọc được bằng https

-> dump code về máy = tool git dumper

docs.text:
Sau khi có code thì mọi chuyện sáng tỏ vì sao fuzzing file extension 0 được

thư viện có 2 hàm lọc chính là clean() và blocked(). xử lý khá sạch sẽ nên 0 upload được file có ích lên

rename.php sử dụng hàm blocked và clean để làm sạch bất cứ cái tên nào được dùng để rename từ phía user

upload cũng tương tự

tuy nhiên nếu để ý kĩ ta sẽ thấy 1 hàm xử lý trùng lặp khá bcuoi ở đây

vòng while sẽ còn tiếp tục nếu tìm thấy file có đường dẫn (và tên) y hệt mình, trim phần extension cuối cùng ra (ví dụ nếu file là abc.txt thì sẽ trim phần .txt ra, còn nếu không có thì giữ nguyên và báo lỗi 0 ghi được, để tránh trim mãi thành vòng lặp vô hạn).

nếu tên vẫn không giống nhau, thì gán đè lên luôn

-> ta có thể làm trò upload 2 file evil.php.txt lên. vì 2 file có tên y hệt nhau, khi file thứ 2 được tải lên sẽ ghi đè lên file thứ 1, cắt được đuôi .txt dùng để bypass BLOCK_EXT và file evil.php sẽ nằm trong /uploads chờ được execute

lúc này ta quay lại với hint2, anh iu trungtqt đã gợi ý về file .htaccess và nó cho ta biết rằng mọi file ở trong uploads này nếu extension dính 'ph' sẽ không được phép execute. vì thế ta cần upload 1 file .htaccess cho phép chạy .php để ghi đè lên file gốc của hệ thống

rõ ràng là ta không thể bình mới rượu cũ, upload 1 file .htaccess lên để nó ghi đè vào file .htaccess gốc được, vì cái vòng lặp while trong upload.php sẽ chặt mất đuôi .htaccess khi thấy có 2 file trùng nhau. may mắn là file rename.php thì cho rename và ghi đè thẳng lên file gốc, và trong danh sách BLOCKED_EXT cũng không ban .htaccess

-> upload file .htaccess với một cái tên không bị block (E.g: htaccess-override.txt) và rename nó thành .htaccesss bằng /rename.php

việc còn lại là soạn code php để lấy flag từ /var/www/flag1.txt như hint3 (mình ai slop đoạn này) và kích hoạt nó.

docs.title: Wu
docs.text:
basically they use UD2 for a anti-reverse engineering technique. The UD2 instruction is an undefined instruction in x86 architecture that causes the CPU to generate an invalid opcode exception when executed.

but then in the main func, the logic is designed to catch this exception and let the func 'segill_sigaction' handle it.

check the 'segill_sigaction' func, it basically move the register that holds value of the instruction pointer (RIP) to the next instruction after the UD2, effectively skipping over the UD2 instruction and allowing the program to continue executing normally.

docs.title: Reverse Engineering 101: Fundamentals Note
docs.text: Topic: Reverse Engineering & Binary Analysis Fundamentals Key Tools: Ghidra, IDA Pro, GDB, C, Python (ctypes)

docs.title: Basic Data Types and Sizes
docs.text: When source code compiles to machine instructions, high-level abstractions (variable names, types, structs, signedness) are stripped away. The CPU and memory operate strictly on raw bytes and register widths.

docs.title: Quick Reference Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Name Size C Equivalent x86_64 Registers Common Usage / Value Range Byte 1 byte (8 bits) char, uint8_t, int8_t al, bl, cl, dl, r8b ASCII characters, boolean flags (0 to 255 / -128 to 127) Word 2 bytes (16 bits) short, uint16_t, int16_t ax, bx, cx, dx, r8w Short integers, UTF-16 characters Dword (Double Word) 4 bytes (32 bits) int, uint32_t, long (Win32) eax, ebx, ecx, edx, r8d Standard integers, loop counters, 32-bit pointers Qword (Quad Word) 8 bytes (64 bits) long long, uint64_t, pointers rax, rbx, rcx, rdx, r8 64-bit pointers (memory addresses), 64-bit integers

docs.title: Ghidra undefined Types
docs.text:
When Ghidra detects data or a variable but cannot yet infer whether it is a signed/unsigned int, float, pointer, or struct, it assigns a placeholder type:

  • Format: undefinedN where N = byte size.
    • undefined1 $\rightarrow$ 1 byte (Byte)
    • undefined2 $\rightarrow$ 2 bytes (Word)
    • undefined4 $\rightarrow$ 4 bytes (Dword)
    • undefined8 $\rightarrow$ 8 bytes (Qword)
  • Ghidra Tip: Highlight the variable and press Ctrl+L (or right-click $\rightarrow$ Retype Variable) to assign the real type (e.g. int, char*) once you figure out how it is used.

docs.title: How srand(), rand(), and time() work
docs.text: Computers are deterministic machines and cannot generate true random numbers on their own. Instead, standard C libraries use a Pseudo-Random Number Generator (PRNG) algorithm.

docs.title: Mental Model: The Pre-Printed Book
docs.text:
• The PRNG: Imagine a giant book filled with billions of pre-determined numbers in a fixed order.
  • rand(): Reads the next number in the book and advances to the next position.
  • srand(seed): Selects which page to open. Given the exact same seed, the program opens to the exact same page every single run.
  • time(NULL): Returns the current UNIX epoch time (seconds since January 1, 1970). Because this number increments once every second, it is frequently used as a dynamic seed.

docs.title: Typical Pattern in C
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>

int main() {
    // Seed the PRNG with the current timestamp in seconds
    srand((unsigned int)time(NULL));

    // Generates numbers according to the chosen seed
    printf("%d\n", rand());
    printf("%d\n", rand());
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3. Endianness (Byte Ordering)
docs.text:
x86 and x86_64 architectures use Little Endian representation: the least significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address.

  • Little Endian (x86 / ARM default):
    • Value: 0x12345678
    • Stored in memory as: \x78 \x56 \x34 \x12
  • Big Endian (Network Byte Order):
    • Value: 0x12345678
    • Stored in memory as: \x12 \x34 \x56 \x78
  • RE Note: When inspecting raw hex in Ghidra or Hex Editors, multi-byte constants appear reversed compared to their numeric representation.

docs.title: Write up
docs.text:
Link to the challenge: Simple Encryptor

first, i put the encrypt file inside Ghidra. after that, Ghidra decompiles the binary file back into a c/c++ language code.

after that lets focus on explaining lines of code 

local_30 = fopen("flag","rb");
fseek(local_30,0,2);
local_28 = ftell(local_30);
fseek(local_30,0,0);
local_20 = malloc(local_28);
fread(local_20,local_28,1,local_30);
fclose(local_30);

this part can be understood as opening a file stream, allocating memory for the file content, reading the content into memory, and then closing the file stream.

tVar2 = time((time_t *)0x0);
local_40 = (uint)tVar2;
srand(local_40);

time((time_t *)0x0) means time(NULL) which returns the current time in seconds since the epoch January 1, 1970.

This value is then used to seed the random number generator with srand local_40.

How srand(), rand(), and time() work will be explained in Fundamentals/re_101.md.

for (local_38 = 0; local_38 < (long)local_28; local_38 = local_38 + 1) {
  iVar1 = rand();
  *(byte *)((long)local_20 + local_38) = *(byte *)((long)local_20 + local_38) ^ (byte)iVar1;
  local_3c = rand();
  local_3c = local_3c & 7;
  *(byte *)((long)local_20 + local_38) =
        *(byte *)((long)local_20 + local_38) << (sbyte)local_3c |
        *(byte *)((long)local_20 + local_38) >> 8 - (sbyte)local_3c;
}

main part of the encryption algorithm is a for loop that iterates through each byte of the file content stored in local_20.

I can rewrite the code in a more readable way:

  for (int i = 0; i < file_size; i++) {
    int random_value = rand();
    file_content[i] ^= (byte)random_value; // XOR operation with a random value
    int shift_amount = rand() & 7;
    file_content[i] = (file_content[i] << shift_amount) | (file_content[i] >> (8 - shift_amount)); // Bitwise rotation
  }

So basically the encryption algorithm goes like this:

  1. XOR each byte with random_value.

  2. Bitwise rotate the result by shift_amount.

We can reverse the encryption process like this:

  1. Bitwise rotate the encrypted byte by (8 - shift_amount).

  2. XOR the result with the same random_value.

local_18 = fopen("flag.enc","wb");
fwrite(&local_40,1,4,local_18);
fwrite(local_20,1,local_28,local_18);
fclose(local_18);

after we know how the encryption algorithm works & how to reverse it, we just need to know what is the random value (seed) that was used to encrypt the file.

luckily, the program saves the seed value local_40 into the first 4 bytes of the encrypted file flag.enc.

now the only thing left to do is to read the first 4 bytes of the encrypted flag.enc file, and use that value to seed the random number generator again, and then we can decrypt the file by reversing the encryption process.

i can extract 4 bytes from the encrypted flag.enc file by writing a simple script in python:

import struct
with open('flag.enc', 'rb') as f:
    # Read 4 bytes, unpack as Little-Endian (<) Unsigned Integer (I)
    seed = struct.unpack('<I', f.read(4))[0] 
    print(f"The seed is: {seed}")

The result of the script:

So the seed is 1655780698. I can check if this is correct by reading flag.enc file using a hex editor.

we can see that the first 4 bytes of the flag.enc file is 5A 35 B1 62.

however, the value is stored in Little-Endian format, so we need to reverse the byte order to get the correct seed value.

-> The correct seed value is 62 B1 35 5A in hex, which is 0x62B1355A = 1655780698 in decimal.

After we have the seed value, we can use it to seed the random number generator again and then decrypt the file by reversing the encryption process.

I wrote a simple C script to do this:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>


int main() {
    // Read the encrypted file
    FILE *file = fopen("flag.enc", "rb"); 
    fseek(file, 0, SEEK_END);
    long file_size = ftell(file);
    fseek(file, 0, SEEK_SET);
    uint8_t *file_content = malloc(file_size);
    fread(file_content, 1, file_size, file);
    fclose(file);

    srand(1655780698); // Seed the random number generator with the known seed

    // Decrypt the file
    // Notice that the first 4 bytes of the file (0 - 3) are the seed value and didn't get encrypted -> we start from 4.
    for (int i = 4; i < file_size; i++) {
        int random_value = rand(), shift_amount = rand() & 7;
        file_content[i] = (file_content[i] >> shift_amount) | (file_content[i] << (8 - shift_amount)); // Reverse bitwise rotation
        file_content[i] ^= (uint8_t)random_value; // XOR operation with the same random value
    }

    FILE *output_file = fopen("flag.txt", "wb");

    fwrite(file_content + 4, 1, file_size - 4, output_file); // Print ONLY the decrypted content into flag.txt
    fclose(output_file);
    free(file_content);

    return 0;
}

This part i bumped into a problem. Because encrypt is a Linux ELF binary, it uses the glibc implementation of rand().

I ran decrypt.c on Windows, but the rand() implementation on Windows uses ucrtbase.dll implementation, which is different from the one in glibc. So the decrypted content is not correct.

because of that I ran decrypt.c in WSL. We found the flag.

Flag: 

HTB{vRy_s1MplE_F1LE3nCryp0r}

docs.title: Write up
docs.text:
Platform: Hack The Box Category: Reverse Engineering Difficulty: Very Easy Challenge Link: Spooky Pass

First impression:

I opened the pass file using hex editor and found that it was an ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) file.

We can see 7F 45 4C 46 or ELF in the first 4 bytes of the file. This is a common signature for ELF files.

So I put the pass file inside Ghidra. after that, Ghidra decompiles the binary file back into a c/c++ language code.

P.S. We can see the password right away in the hex editor. But for the sake of learning, let's continue with reading the decompiled code.

Let's analyze the decompiled main function:

puts("Welcome to the \x1b[1;3mSPOOKIEST\x1b[0m party of the year.");
printf("Before we let you in, you\'ll need to give us the password: ");
fgets(local_98,0x80,stdin);
pcVar2 = strchr(local_98,10);
if (pcVar2 != (char *)0x0) {
*pcVar2 = '\0';
}
iVar1 = strcmp(local_98,"s3cr3t_p455_f0r_gh05t5_4nd_gh0ul5");
if (iVar1 == 0) {
puts("Welcome inside!");
for (local_c4 = 0; local_c4 < 0x1a; local_c4 = local_c4 + 1) {
    local_b8[(int)local_c4] = (char)*(undefined4 *)(parts + (long)(int)local_c4 * 4);
}
puts(local_b8);
}
else {
puts("You\'re not a real ghost; clear off!");
}

The program logic is simple:

  1. Print a welcome message & ask for the password.

  2. Compare the password with s3cr3t_p455_f0r_gh05t5_4nd_gh0ul5.

  3. If the password is correct, print "Welcome inside!" and local_b8 which is constructed from parts array.

local_b8 is 99% sure the flag. There are two ways to get the flag.

First way is to run the program and input the correct password.

The second way is to get the flag from the parts array. The parts array is located at 00104060. The current data stored inside is undefined, so I'm gonna give it the type dword - we can easily see the pattern of 0 bytes -> each value is 4 bytes (for more details on basic data types, go to Fundamentals/re_101.md).

So I changed the type of parts to dword and then I can see the values stored inside.

Flag: 

HTB{un0bfu5c4t3d_5tr1ng5}
